items.headline: Thirteen killed in a day as Israeli tanks push west of the yellow line in Deir al-Balah
items.fact: Gaza's civil defence said Israeli fire and air strikes killed at least 13 people and wounded about 60 in 24 hours, as Israeli armour advanced west of the yellow line in Deir al-Balah.
items.standfirst: Residents of central Gaza say troop movements across the ceasefire line force them out of homes and shelters, only for some to return when the forces pull back. Israel says it is striking militants who violate the truce.
body: Israeli tanks and military vehicles moved westward beyond the so-called yellow line in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, The New Arab reported on Monday. Residents fear the forces could reach Salah al-Din Street, the territory's main north-south road.

Mahmoud Bassal, spokesperson for Gaza's civil defence, said at least 13 people had been killed and around 60 wounded across the Strip over the previous 24 hours. Two of the dead were killed when a vehicle was struck in Deir al-Balah in the afternoon.

Hamas said two members of its security apparatus were killed on what it called a security mission in central Gaza. The Israeli military said separately that its strikes on Saturday and Sunday killed four operatives, including two Islamic Jihad members, whom it accused of acting in systematic violation of the ceasefire.
The New Arab put the overall death toll in Gaza since October 2023 at 74,555. Estimates cited by the outlet suggest Israel now controls nearly two-thirds of the territory.
A Gaza-based analyst linked the escalation to Israel's general election, held on Tuesday.

context.text: Under the October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces pulled back to the yellow line, which roughly splits the Strip into east and west. The UN says new yellow blocks have since been seen in Ash Shuja'iyyeh and parts of Deir al-Balah, and Israeli control has grown beyond the 53% the deal allowed.

voices.quote: These movements have forced residents to flee their homes and shelters, only to return when the forces pull back.

items.headline: Strikes on Islamic University campus kill three guards and wound seven students
items.fact: An Israeli air strike on the Islamic University campus in Gaza City killed three security guards, hours after a drone strike there wounded seven female students.
items.standfirst: The campus was hit twice on Sunday, a day on which at least eight Palestinians were killed across the Strip. Most university buildings had already been destroyed earlier in the war.
body: A drone strike on the Islamic University in Gaza City on Sunday wounded seven female students with shrapnel, one of them seriously, Al Jazeera reported. A later air strike on the campus killed three security guards.
The university suspended academic and administrative work after the first attack. Al Jazeera's correspondent said most campus buildings were already in ruins before Sunday.

Elsewhere, two people were killed by shelling in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, according to Nasser Medical Complex, and further deaths were reported east of Deir al-Balah, on al-Rashid Street in the north and in the Sheikh Nasser area of Khan Younis.
The Israeli military did not comment on the campus strikes in the reports reviewed.

items.headline: Girl among three reported killed in strike on al-Mawasi displacement area
items.fact: Hamas-affiliated media reported that an Israeli strike in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, killed three people including a girl; Israel later said it hit three militants leaving a tunnel nearby.
items.standfirst: The coastal area of al-Mawasi shelters large numbers of displaced families. The Times of Israel said it could not independently verify the casualty report.
body: Three people, including a girl, were killed in an Israeli strike in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, according to Hamas-affiliated media cited by The Times of Israel early on Monday. The Israeli military did not immediately comment.
Later the same day the military said it had struck three operatives who came out of a tunnel shaft west of the yellow line in Khan Younis, saying hits were identified but not confirming deaths.
The day before, two people were killed by shelling in al-Mawasi, according to Nasser Medical Complex.

context.text: The yellow line marks the positions Israeli forces withdrew to under the October 2025 ceasefire. Areas west of it, including al-Mawasi, are where most of Gaza's displaced population now lives.

items.headline: WFP cuts Gaza food aid by a third as funding runs short before winter
items.fact: The World Food Programme said funding shortfalls had forced it to cut food assistance in Gaza by about a third, leaving half a million people without its support.
items.standfirst: The agency now reaches 1.1 million people, down from 1.6 million a month earlier, and has halved rations for those it still serves. It says it needs $450 million to keep operating in Gaza and the West Bank until March.
body: WFP said on 19 October that families still receiving food parcels will get one instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour.
Daily hot meals supported by the agency fell from 250,000 to 150,000, and the value of cash assistance to 75,000 families was reduced.
The agency said WFP's 2026 funding for Palestine is less than half the level of previous years. It warned that modest recent gains in food security remain fragile as winter approaches.
About 1.4 million people, or 67% of Gaza's population, are in IPC Phase 3 or worse, down from 1.6 million at the end of 2025, according to WFP.

context.text: OCHA says food security partners reached about 1.3 million people in September, down from 2.1 million in January, and expects monthly reach to fall below one million from October.

items.headline: UN aid trucks rise at Kerem Shalom while commercial deliveries fall by a quarter
items.fact: OCHA said 702 UN and partner trucks were offloaded at Kerem Shalom in the week to 19 October, up 47%, while commercial truckloads fell 25% after a reported halt over a disputed fee.
items.standfirst: Kerem Shalom is the only cargo crossing into Gaza still operating. Aid groups warn their monthly food reach will drop below one million people from October.
body: Of 779 manifested UN and partner trucks, 702 were offloaded at Kerem Shalom between 13 and 19 October, a 47% increase on the week before, OCHA said in its 22 October report.
Commercial truckloads fell by a quarter to 315 between 12 and 18 October, following reports of a halt linked to a disputed fee.
Food security partners reached about 1.3 million people in September, compared with 2.1 million in January, and expect to reach fewer than one million a month from October.
About 60% of the $283 million the shelter cluster needs for the cold and rainy season is unfunded, and 11 water partners may have to stop trucking drinking water.

context.text: Kerem Shalom has been the only operating cargo crossing since Zikim closed on 24 May, according to OCHA.

items.headline: Tents set alight along the yellow line as new markers appear in Shuja'iyyeh
items.fact: The UN said tents were set on fire in Ash Shuja'iyyeh on Sunday night, leaving at least nine households without shelter, as new yellow blocks were seen there and in Deir al-Balah.
items.standfirst: Aid agencies report continued arson along the ceasefire line, and a UN site in Deir al-Balah came under fire. An earlier fire displaced about 200 families.
body: Reported arson attacks are continuing in areas along the yellow line, UN News said on 26 October, citing humanitarian partners.
New yellow blocks were seen in Ash Shuja'iyyeh, in eastern Gaza City, and in parts of Deir al-Balah. Tents burned in Ash Shuja'iyyeh on Sunday night left at least nine households without shelter.
A UN site in Deir al-Balah also came under fire, the UN said.
OCHA had reported on 15 October that Israeli forces moved yellow line markers westward near Ash Shuja'iyyeh on 11 October, raising fears of further displacement.

context.text: The yellow line marks where Israeli forces withdrew under the October 2025 ceasefire. Moving its markers westward shrinks the area where displaced Palestinians can live.

items.headline: Albania signs up to Gaza stabilisation force as planned base waits on Israel
items.fact: Albania has finalised its agreement to join the International Stabilisation Force in Gaza, with liaison officers expected in November, while a planned ISF base near the yellow line remains on hold.
items.standfirst: Up to 500 Moroccan personnel have trained for the force and Kosovo says its bomb disposal team is ready, but a Board of Peace official says Israeli obstruction has stalled the base meant to house them.
body: Albania has completed its participation agreement with the International Stabilisation Force (ISF), and its liaison officers are expected in November, The Times of Israel reported on 26 October.
Kosovo's defence ministry said its explosive ordnance disposal team would deploy once the ISF is ready to receive it.

Up to 500 Moroccan personnel began ISF-led training in Morocco around late August, a Board of Peace official told The Times of Israel, as reported by The New Arab on 20 October. The official could not confirm the training was complete.
A proposed ISF base near the yellow line, intended for about 150 personnel, is on hold because of Israel, the official said.
Morocco said in February it would join the force, the first Arab country to do so publicly. Kazakhstan has also agreed to contribute.

context.text: The ISF is meant to keep order and secure Gaza's borders under the Board of Peace plan, working with a new Palestinian police force as Israel withdraws in stages tied to Hamas disarmament.

next.text: Albanian liaison officers are expected in November; no date has been given for troops to enter Gaza.

items.headline: Hamas warned of a new October 7-style attack in message passed through UN official, Israel says
items.fact: Israel's COGAT said Hamas used UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov to relay an unusually blunt warning that it could carry out another attack like 7 October 2023.
items.standfirst: Hamas reportedly blamed Israeli strikes, the shifting yellow line and the cancellation of Palestinian elections for eroding its position. Israel insists it will not withdraw until Hamas disarms.
body: Senior Hamas officials met Alakbarov at his Gaza office and asked him to pass on the warning, Ynet reported. The UN official then met Maj Gen Yoram Halevy, head of Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), on a Wednesday.
According to the report, Hamas cited Israeli operations in Gaza, moves of the yellow line and the Palestinian Authority's postponement of elections as reasons it was losing control on the ground.

Ynet also reported that Hamas needs about 90 million shekels a month to pay roughly 30,000 personnel, and that Israel is blocking entry to Gaza for the technocratic committee and Palestinian police force.
The account comes from Israeli officials and has not been independently verified.

voices.quote: This is an unusual threat message, which hasn't been previously conveyed in this level of bluntness and directness.

items.headline: A year into the truce, up to 10,000 bodies are thought to remain under Gaza's rubble
items.fact: Gaza civil defence officials say about 1,000 bodies have been recovered since the ceasefire, while an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 are still buried, about 3,000 of them in areas held by the Israeli army.
items.standfirst: Recovery teams are digging by hand and with scarce machinery through the ruins. A large share of the missing lie beyond their reach, behind Israeli lines.
body: France 24's Observers team reported on 23 October on efforts to recover bodies from beneath destroyed buildings a year after the ceasefire.
Civil defence officials say around 1,000 bodies have been recovered so far.
Between 8,000 and 10,000 bodies are believed to remain under the rubble, about 3,000 of them in areas under Israeli army control.

items.headline: Nearly a million displaced Gazans live in sites at risk of flooding, UN says
items.fact: OCHA said about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza live in sites at medium to high risk of flooding, more than 400,000 of them at high risk, with winter shelter needs 66% unfunded.
items.standfirst: Supplies on hand could partly help only 18% of the 294,250 families needing winter shelter aid, and about 8,600 shelter kits remain blocked from entry.
body: In its 15 October report, OCHA said around 950,000 displaced people were living in sites assessed as being at medium to high risk of flooding, including more than 400,000 at high risk.

Available stocks could partially assist only 18% of the 294,250 families who need winter shelter support. Shelter needs were 66% unfunded and roughly 8,600 emergency shelter kits were blocked from entering.
About 44,000 people live in more than 2,300 structurally unsafe buildings.
The report also said 44% of surveyed households had gone to bed hungry at least once in the previous 30 days.

items.headline: Israel says strikes killed two men it accuses of moving millions of shekels to Hamas
items.fact: The Israeli military said strikes last week in Gaza City and Nuseirat killed a Hamas cell commander and an Islamic Jihad operative it accused of transferring millions of shekels to Hamas.
items.standfirst: Israel describes such strikes as responses to ceasefire violations; Gaza's health ministry counts more than 1,500 people killed since the truce began.
body: The military named the men as Alaa Ibrahim Nimer Arshi, a cell commander in Hamas's armed wing, killed in Gaza City on Wednesday, and Karam Riyad Hassan Abu Butaihan, of Palestinian Islamic Jihad, killed in Nuseirat on Tuesday.
It said it had also bombed three Hamas weapons depots in central Gaza on Thursday.
On 26 October the military said it had killed two more Hamas officers, Mohammed Halawa and Ahmed Zahir Fuad Abu-Odeh, accusing them of acting in systematic violation of the ceasefire.

context.text: Haaretz reported Israeli intelligence assessments that Hamas has no plans to disarm and is rebuilding its forces, The Times of Israel said on 22 October. Israel says it will not withdraw further until Hamas disarms.

items.headline: The Gaza ceasefire, one year on: what phase two promised and why it has stalled
items.fact: A year after the October 2025 truce, hostages are home and rockets have stopped, but Hamas has not disarmed, Israel has not withdrawn and Israeli control has grown from 53% of Gaza to around 70%.
items.standfirst: Phase one swapped hostages for prisoners and drew the yellow line. Phase two was meant to move Gaza from Hamas rule to a technocratic committee, an international force and staged Israeli withdrawal tied to disarmament.
body: Phase one: Hamas freed the 20 remaining living hostages within days of the October 2025 deal in exchange for Palestinian prisoners, and no rocket attacks have come from Gaza since, AFP reported on the anniversary. Israeli forces pulled back to the yellow line, which roughly divides the Strip east from west.

Phase two: under the Board of Peace roadmap Hamas accepted at the end of July, weapons would be stored under a Palestinian committee, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) would take power in stages, and an International Stabilisation Force would work with a new Palestinian police. The board's envoy, Nickolay Mladenov, said withdrawal must move in lockstep with decommissioning.

Where it stands: Israel insists on full, verified disarmament first; Hamas has not begun to disarm. Israel has expanded its hold to about 70% of the Strip by official accounts. Albania, Kosovo, Kazakhstan and Morocco have committed to the ISF, but none has deployed.

Money: Trump promised $10 billion in January and donors pledged $17 billion in February, but AFP reported no reconstruction funds are known to have reached Gaza. The board proposed a $2.45 billion six-month recovery plan in September.
Cost: Gaza's health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable, counted 1,522 Palestinians killed between the truce and 19 October 2026.

context.text: The yellow line is marked by earthen berms, yellow-painted concrete blocks and military posts running about 65 km from Rafah to Beit Hanoun. Residents are barred from approaching it, and it cuts off most of Gaza's farmland.

next.text: Mediators had seen little chance of a breakthrough before Israel's 27 October election; the result, and whether the ISF begins to deploy from November, will shape what comes next.

items.headline: Nearly 4,000 Palestinians forced from their homes in Hebron after checkpoint attack
items.fact: Israel's operation in Hebron, launched after two soldiers were killed at a checkpoint on 23 October, had displaced about 3,971 Palestinians by Monday, according to WAFA.
items.standfirst: Israeli forces sealed the Ein Deir Baha and al-Jilda neighbourhoods, went house to house and began demolitions. The prime minister vowed to change the area completely.
body: Two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli military checkpoint near Hebron on Friday 23 October, killing two soldiers and wounding three. Both gunmen were killed.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel would lock down Hebron, search house to house and demolish homes. A Reuters reporter saw bulldozers begin demolishing homes near the shooting site; residents said the homes had no link to the attackers.

By Monday, WAFA counted about 3,971 people displaced, including around 200 children under two, 258 elderly people and 137 pregnant women. A local relief committee said 619 families were affected and 266 had no safe place to stay.
Hebron's governor said Israeli authorities had set up 128 gates and 120 checkpoints across the governorate. The Palestinian Prisoners' Club reported more than 80 arrests.

Defence Minister Israel Katz said residents would not return until Israel had finished dealing with Hamas in Hebron. Israel said it needed to demolish civilian infrastructure so militants could not use it.

context.text: Netanyahu and Katz compared the operation to the 2025 demolitions in northern West Bank refugee camps, which expelled tens of thousands of people and which Human Rights Watch said amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity.

voices.quote: We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely.

next.text: The IDF said the operation would last several days; Israel has given no date for residents to return.

items.headline: Army chief saw no reason to continue Hebron raid, but Netanyahu ordered it on
items.fact: Israel's public broadcaster Kan reported that army chief Eyal Zamir told Netanyahu there was no operational justification to continue the Hebron operation, and the prime minister ordered it to continue.
items.standfirst: The military had wanted to announce a wind-down as early as Saturday night, according to Kan. The disagreement surfaced a day before Israel's general election.
body: Zamir recommended on Sunday that the operation end because its objectives had been met, Kan reported, as cited by The New Arab. Netanyahu rejected the advice.
Soldiers quoted in Israeli media complained that they were wasting time; one said some had not been home for 28 days.
Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu cancelled a Likud faction meeting, citing security matters.
The IDF said troops had found a tunnel about 15 metres deep near a gunman's home, scanned more than 500 buildings and detained about 50 suspects.

voices.quote: Right now, we're just wasting time.
voices.role: serving in Hebron, quoted by Israeli media

items.headline: Israel seals all West Bank land crossings for election day
items.fact: Israel said it would close all land crossings with the West Bank on 27 October, election day, and barred Palestinian workers from settlements from 25 October.
items.standfirst: About 9,000 Palestinians hold permits to work in settlements. The closures follow the Hebron attack and come alongside a wider lockdown of the territory.
body: All land crossings with the West Bank will close on election day, France 24 reported, citing AFP.
From Sunday the army barred Palestinian workers from entering Israeli communities and restricted their movement across the West Bank, including to industrial zones.
The Times of Israel reported that about 9,000 Palestinians hold permits to work in settlements and that crossings would reopen after election day.
Over Friday and Saturday the army said it operated in 40 areas and detained about 40 suspects it linked to Hamas and Islamic Jihad.

voices.quote: Anyone who messes with us will quickly understand that he will pay a painful price.

next.text: Crossings are due to reopen after the vote.

items.headline: Settlers burn olive trees in Abu Falah and beat a Washington Post photographer
items.fact: About 80 settlers attacked olive pickers in Abu Falah, setting trees alight and throwing rocks; Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was among those injured.
items.standfirst: Levine suffered broken ribs and vertebrae and a nearly severed finger. A similar attack the same morning in Turmus Ayya ended with three cars burned.
body: Some of the settlers carried gas canisters, France 24 reported. Israeli military jeeps arrived during the attack and soldiers fired tear gas; a Reuters photographer saw an armed settler fire a gun.
The army said troops fired warning shots and at one point fired towards a person they believed posed a threat.
Levine said she was pushed to the ground and kicked while wearing a flak jacket and helmet. AP later reported she suffered broken ribs and vertebrae, a nearly severed finger and stab-like wounds.
In nearby Turmus Ayya the same morning, settlers attacked farmers and burned three cars.

items.headline: Israeli police arrest 10 after weekend settler attacks on journalist and diplomats
items.fact: Israeli police said they arrested 10 people on 19 October over a wave of settler violence that included attacks on a Washington Post photographer and European diplomats.
items.standfirst: Police did not name the suspects or describe their roles. Rights groups say attackers are rarely arrested or punished.
body: The Shin Bet, Border Police and military took part in the investigation, police said. The operation also targeted suspected breaches of a closed military zone order and illegal construction.
Heidi Levine said she was shocked and insulted that Netanyahu had described the attack on her as alleged.
The arrests followed condemnation from the United States and European governments.

voices.quote: Impunity for violent settlers must end.

context.text: OCHA documented 2,159 settler attacks in 2026 up to 19 October, an average of 7.4 a day compared with five a day in 2025.

items.headline: Settlers are picking and pressing Palestinian olives as harvest attacks grow, rights group says
items.fact: Yesh Din recorded 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters and 168 cases of crop theft in the first 24 days of the season, with Israeli forces present in at least a quarter.
items.standfirst: In Lubban al-Gharbi a villager watched his olives taken. An Israeli government spokesperson said olives picked by a Jew in the Jewish ancestral homeland were not theft.
body: Reuters reported from Lubban al-Gharbi, where villager Ahmed Salem's olives were taken by settlers.
Yesh Din's figures cover the first 24 days of the harvest. Palestinian authorities say three Palestinians have been killed in settler attacks this season.
Reuters said olive oil from Avichai Farm, a settler outpost with its own press, sells for about $20 a bottle. A rabbi from the Alon Shvut settlement condemned the theft.
An Israeli government spokesperson argued the picking was not theft while saying no one should take the law into their own hands. The military said it takes violence seriously.

items.headline: Harvest-season settler attacks already exceed the totals for 2024 and 2025, UN says
items.fact: OCHA documented 272 olive-harvest-related settler attacks between 1 September and 19 October, more than in the whole 2024 (224) or 2025 (185) seasons.
items.standfirst: The attacks killed one Palestinian, injured 200 and damaged more than 3,200 olive trees and saplings. The UN human rights office called it an ominous start to the season.
body: OCHA's 22 October report recorded 83 settler attacks across 48 communities in the week of 13 to 19 October alone.
In the same week, 148 Palestinians were injured, 92 of them by Israeli forces and 56 by settlers, including six children.
The UN human rights office urged states and donors on 21 October to go beyond condemnation, calling for more diplomatic presence in high-risk communities.
UN figures show 286,000 olive trees were damaged in the West Bank between 2023 and the end of September 2026, including 100,000 this year before the harvest began.

items.headline: Farmers report settlers in keffiyehs among those attacking olive groves
items.fact: Palestinian farmers told France 24 that some settlers attacking groves wore keffiyehs, as Israeli rights group B'Tselem said soldiers often stand by while settlers attack and steal.
items.standfirst: Many families started picking two weeks early this year to reduce the risk of violence. The harvest officially runs from 15 October to the end of November.
body: France 24's Observers spoke to farmers in the Hebron governorate and near Birzeit, who gave pseudonyms.
One said they had been barred from their orchard on the grounds it was now a military zone. Another said settlers wearing keffiyehs had come to attack them.
France 24 also found that a widely shared video of trees being ripped up was fake, while noting that real uprooting is well documented.
B'Tselem estimates the olive sector is worth about $170 million a year to Palestinians.

items.fact: Rabbis for Human Rights said Israeli soldiers used a closed military zone order signed the same day to remove its activists and Palestinian farmers from an olive grove near Huwara.
items.standfirst: The same day, WAFA reported a 58-year-old woman beaten and injured in the chest in a settler attack near as-Samu, south of Hebron.

Near as-Samu, south of Hebron, two Palestinians were injured in a settler attack, WAFA said. One, 58-year-old Hakima Halaia, was hurt in the chest after being beaten.

items.fact: A Jerusalem court released settlement security coordinator Pinhas Shem Tov Ran to house arrest in the Golan Heights; he is accused of seriously wounding an 18-year-old Palestinian woman at an unauthorised roadblock.
items.standfirst: The court cited conflicting accounts and a lack of footage. The prosecution had asked for him to stay in custody.
body: The Jerusalem Magistrate's Court ruled on 26 October, The Times of Israel reported.
The woman's father told Kan that Ran fired 10 rounds. She was seriously wounded.
The incident took place at a roadblock that was not authorised, near the Gidonim Ridge, according to the report.

items.headline: House near Jalud set on fire after settlers who took it over clash with soldiers
items.fact: Settlers who had taken over a Palestinian-owned house near Jalud clashed with Israeli soldiers on Saturday, and the house was set on fire; the army said it was dealing with violent rioters at an illegal outpost.
items.standfirst: Jalud's mayor says the house belongs to an East Jerusalem resident. Overnight, settlers also reportedly smashed several Palestinian cars in Sinjil.
body: The IDF said the house sat within an illegal outpost in a closed military zone and described those involved as violent rioters, The Times of Israel reported.
Jalud mayor Raed al-Haj Mohammed said the property belongs to a resident of East Jerusalem.
In Sinjil, near Ramallah, settlers reportedly smashed several Palestinian cars overnight. No injuries were reported.

items.fact: Israel's High Court ordered the state to give a timetable for the steps it says are needed before residents can return to the Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps, with a response due by 23 November.
items.standfirst: The court stopped short of ordering an immediate return or an army withdrawal. The finance minister urged the military not to cooperate with the court.

Justices Isaac Amit, Alex Stein and Khaled Kabub asked the state whether the work could be speeded up and to respond to claims of shortfalls in aid.

items.headline: Why the olive harvest has become the West Bank's most dangerous season
items.fact: The harvest runs from mid-October to the end of November and supports tens of thousands of families; in 2026 harvest-related settler attacks passed the full-season totals of the two previous years by mid-October.
items.standfirst: Olives are income, inheritance and identity for Palestinian villages. Access permits, closed military zones, settler violence and theft now shape who can pick, and when.
body: The season: the harvest officially began on 15 October and runs to the end of November, though many families started two weeks early this year to limit the risk of attack, France 24 reported.

The economy: in 2019 more than 10 million olive trees supported 80,000 to 100,000 families, according to OCHA figures cited by France 24. B'Tselem puts the sector's value at about $170 million a year.
Access: much land near settlements can be reached only with prior coordination with Israeli authorities. That zone grew to about 88,300 dunums in 2026, nearly 30% more than in 2025, OCHA says.

Violence: OCHA counted 272 harvest-related settler attacks between 1 September and 19 October, against 224 in all of 2024 and 185 in 2025. Yesh Din recorded 168 cases of crop theft in the first 24 days.
Losses: the Palestinian agriculture ministry estimates $157 million in losses since October 2023, and says 90% of Gaza's two million olive trees have been destroyed.

context.text: Israeli forces have uprooted or damaged more than 10,000 trees in 2026 and settler attacks have damaged more than 20,000 more, OCHA says.

items.standfirst: The house, built about 15 years ago, was home to al-Rajabi, his wife and five children. The family had already been fined 60,000 shekels.
body: The Wadi Hilweh Information Center said the family carried out the demolition on Sunday after receiving a written order, WAFA reported.
Authorities had earlier fined the family a total of 60,000 shekels for alleged unlicensed building.
Families often demolish their own homes to avoid the extra fees and penalties charged when municipal crews do it, according to OCHA, cited in the report.

items.headline: East Jerusalem Palestinians cannot vote in Israel's election, but live with its results
items.fact: Most Palestinian Jerusalemites hold residency rather than citizenship and cannot vote in Israel's national elections, though policies on housing and policing shape their lives, Haaretz reported.
items.standfirst: Many also boycott municipal elections. In Silwan, one mother of three lives in a home the authorities say was built without a permit.
body: Haaretz spoke to Manal Jalajel, a Silwan resident whose home received a municipal demolition notice about five years ago, written in Hebrew, which she could not read.
The paper said the consequences of Israeli politics, from housing to policing, are hard for Palestinian Jerusalemites to escape.

items.headline: The Al-Aqsa status quo: an unwritten deal now being worn away
items.fact: Under the long-standing status quo, Muslims pray at the compound while non-Muslims may visit only at set times through one gate and may not pray; police now in effect allow Jewish prayer on its eastern side.
items.standfirst: Jordan's Waqf runs religious affairs, Israel controls security, and every shift in the rules is felt across the region.
body: The arrangement: the status quo is vague and unwritten. Muslims can enter and pray with few restrictions. Non-Muslims, including Jews, may visit only in limited time slots through a single gate, and are not supposed to pray, The Times of Israel reports.

Who runs it: Israel captured the site in 1967 but left religious authority with the Islamic Waqf, administered by Jordan. In the 1994 peace treaty Israel recognised Jordan's special role in Muslim holy shrines in Jerusalem.

What has changed: police now de facto permit Jewish prayer on the eastern side, while arrests continue for prayer on the western side. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, who oversees the police, has prayed openly there; Netanyahu's office says the status quo remains in force.
Scale: the Jerusalem Governorate counted 40,661 settler entries between January and August 2026, and Palestinian estimates put Sukkot entries at more than 9,000.
For Palestinians, restrictions have tightened: Waqf guards say they can be barred for six months for looking at a settler, and worshippers report bans over social media posts.

voices.quote: a flagrant violation of the historical and legal status quo
Al-Aqsa is my soul.

items.headline: UN inquiry tells General Assembly Israel continues to commit genocide in Gaza
items.fact: The UN Commission of Inquiry, chaired by Srinivasan Muralidhar, reported to the General Assembly that Israel has committed war crimes and crimes against humanity and continues to commit genocide in Gaza.
items.standfirst: The commission said Israel's expanding control in Gaza keeps killing civilians near the yellow line. Israel rejected the findings as misinformation.
body: The report was presented to the UN General Assembly, UN News said on 26 October. The commission was set up by the Human Rights Council in 2021.
It found that Israel continues to commit genocide in Gaza and has committed war crimes and crimes against humanity in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel's permanent mission in Geneva dismissed the report as part of a campaign to demonise Israel.

Separately, UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese issued a report titled 'Truth under the rubble: media in the time of genocide' on the killing of Palestinian journalists and restrictions on media.

voices.quote: form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians

context.text: In June 2026 the same commission told the Human Rights Council that Israeli forces had deliberately targeted Palestinian children.

items.headline: UN rights chief warns Hebron operation raises concerns of ethnic cleansing
items.fact: UN human rights chief Volker Türk said Israel's Hebron operation, which had forced more than 3,000 people from their homes, raised serious concerns of ethnic cleansing and amounted to collective punishment.
items.standfirst: Speaking in Cairo, Secretary-General António Guterres described an increasingly coercive environment for Palestinians. Türk called for the displaced to be allowed home and compensated.
body: Türk said the operation had demolished homes and commercial property and restricted residents' movement, UN News reported.
He warned of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force and called for the return of displaced residents, with compensation and reparation.
Guterres, in Cairo, warned that the threat of ethnic cleansing was growing.
The Israeli military said the operation would last several days and was limited to the area the attackers came from.

items.headline: Settlers attack European diplomats' convoy in Taybeh and beat a French mayor
items.fact: Masked settlers attacked a convoy carrying Belgian, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives in the Christian village of Taybeh, beating 78-year-old French mayor Bernard Baudoux with iron bars.
items.standfirst: The group had come to help Palestinian farmers with the olive harvest. Belgium and France demanded accountability; Netanyahu said the visit should have been coordinated with the army.
body: Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was kicked and struck but not hospitalised. A local priest said one person needed stitches and an older woman was also beaten, France 24 reported.
France's foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, called the attack appalling and said Israel must urgently halt the violence. Belgium's Maxime Prévot said a Belgian vehicle was damaged.

Netanyahu's office urged caution before drawing conclusions and he later called the episode a smear against settlers. Israel's foreign ministry condemned the incident and police opened an investigation.
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot described the violence as Jewish terrorism under the auspices of the government.

items.headline: Israel detains about 80 olive-harvest volunteers, including a US congressional candidate
items.fact: Israeli forces detained US congressional candidate Brad Lander and about 80 American and Israeli rabbis and activists helping farmers near Nahalin, the largest such detention in a decade, lawyers said.
items.standfirst: Thirty-three of those held were US citizens. Most were released the same day; four activists were to be deported for what Israel called anti-Israel activity.
body: Forces declared a closed military zone near Nahalin, close to the Beitar Illit settlement, and took the volunteers to a police station, NPR reported.
The army said harvesting in the area required prior coordination, which Palestinians had not requested. Israel's foreign ministry called Lander's visit a political stunt.
The New Israel Fund said about 90 volunteers from its Protect the Harvest initiative had been released by Wednesday night. The Times of Israel reported four would be deported.
The US State Department said it was tracking the situation.

items.fact: UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese told Reuters in Jakarta that Indonesia should reconsider its role in Trump's Board of Peace, arguing the rules are set by Israel and Palestinians lack a voice.
items.standfirst: Indonesia has pledged troops to the Gaza stabilisation force. Its foreign ministry says board discussions remain on hold.
body: Albanese recommended Jakarta work instead with the Hague Group, which includes South Africa and Malaysia.
A board official rejected the claim that Palestinians are excluded, pointing to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza led by Ali Shaath.
President Prabowo Subianto has reportedly vowed to quit the board if it does not benefit Palestinians.

items.headline: France rebuffs Ben-Gvir after AI videos mocking Gazans
items.fact: Israeli minister Itamar Ben-Gvir shared AI-generated campaign videos mocking Gazans, including one sending a Palestinian to Paris; France's foreign ministry replied that even magic could not lift his entry ban.
items.standfirst: France barred Ben-Gvir in May over his treatment of activists on a Gaza-bound flotilla. Israel's election rules require AI campaign content to be labelled.
body: One video showed a ruined Gaza in 2030 with a donkey and the message that only a donkey would stay in Gaza, France 24's Truth or Fake team reported.
In another, an elderly Palestinian rubs a magic lamp, summons Ben-Gvir and is sent to Paris.
France's 'French Response' account on X answered with a jibe about his ban, and Ben-Gvir replied with an AI video of himself speaking French.
Deutsche Welle found Likud used AI in about a quarter of the campaign content it analysed.

items.headline: Israel votes in an election seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, with Arab voters pivotal
items.fact: Israelis vote on 27 October in an election framed as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, and France 24 reports that turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel could decide the outcome.
items.standfirst: Arab turnout has traditionally lagged, but some voters say casting a ballot feels more of a duty than ever. Trump has twice urged Israelis to back Netanyahu.
body: France 24 reported that Arab Israeli votes could be crucial to Netanyahu's fate, and that some Arab citizens now see voting as an obligation because of his policies and wars.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the vote and, on 26 October, urged Israelis to vote for him so the two could finish the job, The Times of Israel reported.
Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has pledged to unite the country. Opponents accuse Netanyahu of stoking tension with Iran before the vote, which his office denies.
Most Palestinians in East Jerusalem, who hold residency rather than citizenship, cannot vote.

voices.quote: It's Israel's democracy and Israel's constitution, and that's what counts for me.

items.headline: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections to September 2027
items.fact: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas cancelled legislative elections due in November and set 11 September 2027 for both presidential and legislative votes, blaming Israeli measures and conditions in Gaza.
items.standfirst: Palestinians have not voted nationally since 2005–06. France, which pressed for the vote as part of its recognition of Palestine, said it was essential the elections take place.
body: The decree cited Israeli military operations, settlement expansion, settler violence, movement restrictions and Israel's withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, The Times of Israel and Reuters reported.
It also pointed to conditions in Gaza, the incomplete Israeli withdrawal, slow reconstruction and the absence of international stabilisation forces.
Hamas and Islamic Jihad backed the delay. Israel's foreign minister accused Abbas of deceiving the international community.
Palestinian activist Samer Sinijlawi told France 24 on 15 October the delay was a terrible disappointment.

notes: Al Jazeera pages (aljazeera.com) could not be opened from this environment (connection reset on every attempt), so no fact relies on them directly. The Islamic University item uses Al Jazeera's own text as republished by Yahoo News, which did open. Several promising Al Jazeera stories were dropped for this reason: the 27 October 'Palestine weekly', the Palestine Action protest at the US embassy in London planned for 31 October, Palestinian citizens' turnout estimates, a reported second arson at a Palestinian-American's home in Burqa, and the 26 October report of five killed including a 7-year-old girl.

Reuters and AP sites are blocked to the fetch tool. Reuters copy was read through Al-Monitor republications, and AP copy through PBS NewsHour. The Times of Israel live blogs are very long; facts were taken from the parts that were read, with times converted from Israel time to GMT (GMT+3 until 25 October, GMT+2 after).
Quotes come from the fetch tool's extraction of each page. They are presented as verbatim but were not checked character by character against the original HTML, so re-check them before publishing.

Window: most items fall between 13 and 27 October 2026. These are older: the Abbas election postponement (10 October; it is in because of follow-up coverage on 15 October), the High Court camps ruling (12 October), and background sources in the explainers (June–July 2026 Board of Peace reporting, the February 2026 New Arab piece on the yellow line, the July 2026 Times of Israel piece on the Temple Mount).

The death toll since the ceasefire differs by source and date: OCHA 1,522 (to 19 Oct), Anadolu citing 1,551 and Al Jazeera citing 1,559 (both seen only in search snippets, not opened). The figures list uses OCHA. AFP on 10 October gave about 1,450.

Hebron displacement figures also differ: Katz said about 2,000 on 24 October, the Hebron municipality 3,189 and Türk 'more than 3,000' on 26 October, and WAFA 3,971 by Monday 26 October. The headline number uses WAFA via The New Arab and gives the others as attribution.

Dropped because they were seen only in search snippets: Silwan al-Bustan demolition totals (Ir Amim via The Times of Israel, May 2026), Guterres's September 2026 General Assembly remarks, and the May 2026 EU political agreement on settler sanctions.
The Ynet story on the Hamas threat carries no visible date. Its date of 24 October is inferred from The Times of Israel live blog entry of 25 October, 02:33 Israel time.

The Guterres quote said to be given 'in Cairo' comes from an AFP summary in The Times of Israel's 26 October live blog. A separate search found no other coverage of a Cairo statement, so that setting rests on one source.

World desk is light on diaspora stories. No opened, in-window diaspora item was found beyond the US activists detained at Nahalin. The 31 October London protest is reported only by Al Jazeera, which could not be opened.
OCHA reports dated 22 October include some later details (bakery closures and reopenings on 23–25 October), and these were not used.

Not found in the window despite searching: a new Sheikh Jarrah eviction, any ICJ or ICC ruling or hearing, and a new EU sanctions decision. The latest EU step found is a political agreement in May 2026.
